# shift-router — Full documentation for LLM consumption

> Stop paying flagship prices for routine turns — and stop handing your hardest turns to a cheap model. A judge weighs each turn and routes by expected cost; multi-model fallback chains keep you running; complex tasks are orchestrated by a Smart CTO that delegates to Fast subagents. Two editions: pi-coding-agent and DeepSeek Harness.

## Overview

**shift-router** is a family of task-level model routers. **pi-shift-router** (v1.7.0) is a [pi-coding-agent](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi-coding-agent) extension; **dsh-shift-router** (v0.6.0) is a DeepSeek Harness plugin. Both route every turn to either a fast execution model or a smart judgment model. Before each turn, a small judge — the fast-tier model itself by default — reads the task and returns `fast` or `smart` plus a confidence. The chosen model then drives the whole turn — all thinking, all tool calls, all message content — at that tier's intelligence level. On complex tasks, the Smart tier runs as a CTO that plans and delegates implementation to Fast subagents (task-level orchestration).

### Roles

| Role | Tier | Emoji | What it does for the whole turn | When |
|------|------|-------|----------------------------------|------|
| **Engineer** | Fast | 🦾 | Handles the workload: writes code, runs tests, fixes the bug, follows the established pattern | Routine, well-defined, low stakes |
| **CTO** | Smart | 🧠 | Drives the entire turn when the work is complex: architecture, design review, security audit, multi-step planning, irrecoverable actions, "very deep" reasoning | High stakes, irreversible, ambiguous, or user asks for depth |

The fast tier is **not** a real engineer — it's a model that handles execution; the smart tier is **not** a real CTO — it's the model that handles complex judgment, but it also **does all the work itself** (writes the code, calls the tools, runs the loop). The judge is a small one-shot classification call; the chosen tier then drives the entire agent run.

**Zero behavior change by default** — both tiers start empty. The router does nothing until you assign models via `/router config`.

## How it works

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Input["User sends a message"]
    Input --> Hook["before_agent_start fires"]
    Hook --> Enabled{"Router enabled?"}
    Enabled -->|No| Skip["pi uses default model"]
    Enabled -->|Yes| Judge["LLM Judge (Fast tier's model, JSON mode)"]
    Judge --> Fail{"Judge OK?"}
    Fail -->|No| Fallback["Hold position — stay on current tier"]
    Fail -->|Yes| Decide
    Decide{"Classified as?"}
    Decide -->|Smart & on Fast| Upgrade["UPGRADE → Smart model (immediate)"]
    Decide -->|Fast & on Smart| Trend["Check sliding window"]
    Decide -->|Same as current| Stay["STAY — no switch"]
    Trend --> Stable{"Fast ≥60% of last 5?"}
    Stable -->|Yes| Down["DOWNGRADE → Fast model"]
    Stable -->|No| Stay
    Upgrade & Down --> Failover["On 429/5xx: mark cooldown + switch to next healthy model in tier"]
    Failover & Stay --> Done["Agent processes with selected model"]
```

Three properties that matter:

- **Upgrades are immediate** (Fast → Smart). Quality first.
- **Downgrades need sustained trend** (≥60% of last 5 turns are Fast). Cache protection.
- **One classification per turn.** No thrashing during tool calls.

**JSON-mode enforcement**: OpenAI-compatible APIs use `response_format: { type: "json_object" }`; Anthropic uses assistant prefill `{` to force JSON-start output. While the Judge is in flight, the status bar shows `🧭 judging…`.

### Runtime failover (v0.6.0)

When the primary model hits 429 / 5xx / quota / Token-Plan exhaustion, pi retries first (provider ×3, agent ×3), then the router takes over:

1. Mark the failing model into **exponential-backoff cooldown** (1m → 4m → 16m → 1h → 4h… capped at 6h; a failover-worthy 4xx / 429 / quota starts at 16m).
2. Immediately `setModel` to the next healthy model **in the same tier** (no cross-tier).
3. pi's pending retry continues with the fallback — same-turn failover.
4. Subsequent turns skip cooled models in `before_agent_start`.
5. A 2xx response clears the cooldown; session restart resets everything.

The Judge also walks the full fast-tier chain before giving up, sharing the same cooldown map as routing. Manual override (`/route-force`) always bypasses cooldowns. Auth/config errors (400/401) never trigger failover.

## Judge modes and the expected-cost bar (v1.4.0–v1.7.0)

**Expected cost, not vote counting.** The judge's confidence is read as `pSmart` (`c` for a `smart` verdict, `1 − c` for a `fast` verdict), and the turn runs Smart iff `pSmart ≥ θ`, where `θ = 1 / reworkPenalty` (default R=3 → θ ≈ 0.33). Below `minConfidence` (0.5) the router holds. Upgrades are immediate; downgrades need `downgradeMemory` (default 2) consecutive decisive fast turns. The old `window.threshold` (0.6) and `cacheAware.sameFamilyThreshold` (0.9) defaults are dead — only non-default values act as overrides.

**Gear presets:** `/router eco` (R=2, θ=0.5 — conservative), `/router default` (R=3, θ≈0.33), `/router sport` (R=5, θ=0.2 — eager). Persisted and tab-completable.

**Three judge modes** (`routing.judge.mode`):

| Mode | Source | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `fast-chain` | The Fast tier chain | Default; byte-identical to pre-v1.7.0 behavior |
| `custom` | A dedicated judge chain (`routing.judge.models`) | Edit it like a tier |
| `decision` | A decision model (TypeSafe Jev / System One class) | Beta, opt-in; typed answer with probability, no JSON parse step, ~$0.0001/turn |

**The honest case for the decision model (and against it):** it removes the whole "the judge failed because a model added a comma" class of failures and is cheap (input tokens only). But it is currently slow per verdict (1.4–6.6 s, median ~5 s, while provider capacity ramps) and a September 2026 independent evaluation found decision models behind the best LLM on 14 of 15 annotation tasks. So it is third in the menu, labelled Beta, off by default. Good for batch and background routing; the LLM judge remains the better default for interactive turns.

**Judge availability ladder (v1.7.0):** judge chain → LLM judge → no routing at all. It covers a rotted config (no authenticated endpoint, retired model, removed key) and call-time failures (429/5xx/timeout) in the same turn, for every mode. The last rung behaves as if the plugin were not installed: no model switch, orchestration cleared, session-start model restored, one notice per session. A failed judge call never fabricates a verdict.

## Task-level orchestration (v1.0.0, hardened through v1.5.0)

When the Judge says a task is complex and orchestration is in `auto` mode (default), the router hands the turn to the Smart tier as a **CTO**: it plans the work, delegates implementation to Fast engineer subagents, reviews each result, iterates with concrete feedback, and does a final acceptance pass. Simple tasks (`fast` verdict) never orchestrate — they stay on the plain router.

1. **Enter.** Judge says `smart` → the router switches the main agent to the Smart model and injects an orchestrator instruction. Status shows `🪄 orchestrating`.
2. **Plan.** The Smart agent decomposes the task into phases, each with acceptance criteria.
3. **Delegate.** For each phase it spawns a Fast subagent (`context: "fresh"`, model pinned from the Fast tier) with a self-contained task contract.
4. **Review.** It reads each worker's result against the phase's acceptance criteria; failed phases go back with feedback or are taken over by Smart.
5. **Accept.** Final CTO summary + acceptance pass.

**Hard caps** (the router's part, independent of the Smart agent): `orchestration.maxRounds` (default 3) and `orchestration.escalationThreshold` (default 2 — after N worker failures on a phase, Smart takes over that phase itself). The loop stops when the Smart agent says done or a cap is hit.

**Why fresh-context workers:** workers run with no inherited session history; the task string is their world. Each is small, fast, cheap (~$0.004 narrow task vs ~$0.06 inherited 176k-token fork) and keeps thinking enabled on anthropic-compatible endpoints.

**Convergence protocol (v1.2.0):** every re-delegation must carry a structured `## Failure report` (what failed, where, the exact acceptance test to re-run); re-sending identical feedback is forbidden and triggers a takeover by the Smart CTO.

**Acceptance audit (v1.3.0):** because review is the CTO's own judgment, the router adds a hard fallback audit at the end of every orchestrated turn. Deterministic checks always run (every spawned worker reported back, the final message carries a CTO summary, whether the run ended at a hard cap). An optional small fast-tier LLM audit (`orchestration.audit.enabled`, default on) then checks three dimensions against the captured user goal: **grounding** (acceptance claims backed by results), **goal alignment** (the delivered work addresses the request), and **delivered quality** (no placeholders/empty results passed off as done). Findings never block the finished turn — they surface as `console.warn` + toast and `/router status → Last audit`. The audit only applies to delegated turns (at least one worker spawned); self-executed turns are exempt.

**Per-worker cost attribution (v1.5.0):** each delegated worker's spend lands in a bounded per-worker ledger (last 20, reset per orchestration task), and `/router status` shows an `orchestration $X (N workers)` line — so the cost of delegation is never hidden inside the main-agent figures.

**When it doesn't engage:** simple tasks (`fast` verdict) never orchestrate; without `pi-subagents` installed, complex tasks run directly on the Smart tier exactly as before; `/router orchestrate off` returns to plain two-tier routing. Prerequisite: `pi install npm:pi-subagents`.

## Quick Start

**Prerequisites** — Node.js ≥ 24, pi-agent ≥ 0.80, one provider account with API key in pi-agent's `auth.json`, one model for each tier.

**Install**

```bash
pi install npm:pi-shift-router
```

Registers in `~/.pi/agent/settings.json` and auto-loads on next pi launch. See [pi's packages docs](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi-coding-agent/blob/main/docs/packages.md) for git / local-path install.

**Configure**

Inside pi, run `/router config` and pick one Fast + one Smart model. Save to user or project scope.

**Verify**

`/router status` shows your tiers and models; the next turn triggers the first Judge call.

## Commands

| Command | What it does |
|---------|--------------|
| `/router status` | Open the status dashboard (TUI): live model, last decision + why, tier chains with inline cooldowns, per-model context/cache gauges, money, config layer |
| `/router on` / `/router off` | Enable / disable routing |
| `/router eco\|default\|sport` | Gear presets for the expected-cost bar (persisted) |
| `/router config` | Launch the TUI configuration wizard |
| `/router quiet` | Toggle inline toast notifications |
| `/router verbose` | Toggle verbose console logging (writes to `~/.pi/agent/logs/shift-router.log`, never stdout) |
| `/router orchestrate auto\|off` | Task-level orchestration (default `auto`) or plain two-tier routing |
| `/route-force <tier>` | Pin Smart or Fast for the next turn |
| `/route-force <provider>/<model>` | Pin a specific model for the next turn |
| `/route-force auto` | Clear manual override |

## Configuration

Two-layer config: user (`~/.pi/agent/pi-shift-router.json`) + project (`<cwd>/.pi/pi-shift-router.json`). Project wins on conflict.

```json
{
  "enabled": true,
  "tiers": {
    "fast":  { "models": [
      { "provider": "deepseek", "model": "deepseek-v4-flash", "priority": 1 },
      { "provider": "kimi",     "model": "kimi-k3",          "priority": 2 }
    ] },
    "smart": { "models": [{ "provider": "kimi", "model": "kimi-k3", "priority": 1 }] }
  },
  "routing": { "mode": "auto", "judge": { "mode": "fast-chain" }, "judgeTimeout": 5000, "window": { "minConfidence": 0.5 }, "economics": { "reworkPenalty": 3, "downgradeMemory": 2 }, "cacheAware": { "enabled": true, "sameFamilyPenalty": 1.5 } },
  "orchestration": { "mode": "auto", "maxRounds": 3, "escalationThreshold": 2, "audit": { "enabled": true } },
  "ux": { "quietMode": false, "statusBar": true, "inlineToast": true, "routerLogVerbose": false }
}
```

| Field | Default | Meaning |
|-------|---------|---------|
| `enabled` | `true` | Master switch. Use `/router off` to disable. |
| `tiers.<tier>.models[]` | `[]` | Ordered by `priority`. First hit wins; rest are run-time fallbacks. |
| `routing.judgeTimeout` | `5000` | ms. Judge API call timeout. |
| `routing.judge.mode` | `fast-chain` | Where the verdict comes from: `fast-chain`, `custom` (`routing.judge.models`), or `decision` (a decision model). |
| `routing.window.minConfidence` | `0.5` | Verdict below this = no signal (hold position). |
| `routing.economics.reworkPenalty` | `3` | Wrong-downgrade cost in price-deltas. θ = 1/R. The expected-cost bar. |
| `routing.economics.downgradeMemory` | `2` | Consecutive decisive fast decisions required to downgrade. |
| `routing.cacheAware.sameFamilyPenalty` | `1.5` | θ divisor when both tiers share a provider (fewer downgrades → warm cache survives). |
| `orchestration.mode` / `maxRounds` / `escalationThreshold` | `auto` / `3` / `2` | Task-level orchestration switch + hard caps. |
| `orchestration.audit.enabled` | `true` | Post-turn acceptance audit (deterministic checks + optional LLM audit on grounding / goal alignment / delivered quality). |
| `ux.quietMode` / `statusBar` / `inlineToast` / `routerLogVerbose` | various | Surface controls. |

Each tier's `models` array is an **ordered priority list** — first entry is the primary; later entries stand by as fallback. Configure multiple models via `/router config`'s TUI chain editor (`a` add, `x` remove, `J`/`K` reorder, `d` save, `Esc` cancel).

## FAQ

### What if I don't configure any models?

Both tiers start empty. The router is a no-op; pi uses its default model. Run `/router config`.

### Does the Judge add noticeable latency?

A Judge call costs a few thousand tokens at your Fast-tier pricing. End-to-end classification round-trip is typically 200ms–2s. The status bar shows `🧭 judging…` during the call.

### What if my primary model 429s or times out?

Exponential-backoff cooldown: 5xx starts at 1m (1m → 4m → 16m → 1h → 4h… capped at 6h); a failover-worthy 4xx (429 rate limit / quota) skips the first tiers and starts at 16m, because client-side limits usually outlive server blips. The next healthy model in the same tier takes over — even mid-turn. A 2xx response clears the cooldown.

### Does this work across different providers?

Yes. Each tier stores an ordered list of `{provider, model, priority}` pairs. Mix freely.

### Will it downgrade Smart prematurely?

Only when the router's expected-cost bar is cleared. The turn runs Smart iff `pSmart ≥ θ`, where `θ = 1/reworkPenalty` (default 0.33); a verdict below `minConfidence` (default 0.5) is discarded and the router holds. Downgrades additionally need `downgradeMemory` (default 2) consecutive decisive fast turns, while upgrades are always immediate. Use `/router eco` / `/router sport` to move the bar without touching the math.

### What happens if the judge is unavailable?

The router walks an availability ladder — judge chain, then LLM judge, then no routing at all — for both a rotted config and a call-time failure, in the same turn. The last rung behaves as if the plugin were not installed and says so once per session. It never fabricates a verdict: a fallback verdict used to be treated as a decisive `fast` with full confidence, which could silently downgrade a Smart session after two outages.

### Is there cost overhead from the Judge?

The Judge runs on the Fast-tier model (typically a high value-per-dollar pick). Savings from avoiding unnecessary Smart-tier turns dwarf this cost.

### What is task-level orchestration?

A `smart` verdict on a complex task makes the Smart tier run as a **CTO**: plan → delegate implementation to Fast subagents → review → iterate → accept, then a post-turn acceptance audit. Hard caps (maxRounds 3, escalationThreshold 2) are enforced by the router. Simple tasks (`fast` verdict) never orchestrate. `/router orchestrate off` disables it; it requires the `pi-subagents` extension (pi) or a deployment-pinned worker model (DSH, or run `/router allow-workers on`).

### Does orchestration cost more?

No — the Smart tier plans and reviews; Fast subagents implement in fresh contexts that are small and cheap (~$0.004 for a narrow task vs ~$0.06 for an inherited 176k-token fork). If a task turns out simple, the machinery never engages.

### What keeps an orchestrated turn honest?

Two safety nets. The convergence protocol (v1.2.0) requires every re-delegation to carry a structured failure report (what failed, where, the exact acceptance test to re-run) — re-sending identical feedback is forbidden and the CTO takes the phase over. On top of that, a post-turn acceptance audit (v1.3.0) runs after every orchestrated turn: deterministic checks always run, plus an optional small fast-tier LLM audit of grounding, goal alignment, and delivered quality. Findings never block the finished turn — they surface as `console.warn` + toast and `/router status → Last audit` (`orchestration.audit.enabled`, default on).

### Can I see what routing saves me?

Yes — `/router status` reports cost telemetry: per-tier spend (USD + calls) and a savings baseline. The baseline answers *what would this session have cost if every turn ran on your configured Smart-tier model (priority 1) — i.e. no router?* Example: `Spend: fast $0.045 (9 calls) · smart $0.42 (3 calls) · total $0.465` → `baseline: all-turns-on-smart → $3.21` → `saved $2.74`. If pricing is missing (fully-local session with no `models-store.json` pricing), the baseline shows `unavailable` instead of a made-up number.

## Licensing

- **Author & License** — shift-router family by [green-dalii](https://github.com/green-dalii): pi-shift-router + dsh-shift-router, both licensed under [MIT](LICENSE) © 2026.
- **Direct alternatives** — [OpenRouter Auto Router](https://openrouter.ai/docs/features/auto-router) (zero-config, market-driven, optimizes for quality rather than your bill) and [Cloudflare AI Gateway Dynamic Routing](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ai-gateway/features/dynamic-routing/) (versioned flows with quotas and fallbacks, but it sees requests rather than tasks). For pi-internal routing: [@tenchi4u/pi-bifrost](https://pi.dev/packages/@tenchi4u/pi-bifrost?name=router&type=extension) (7-step rules + history heuristics, 4 tiers, saves subscription quota) and [pi-smart-router](https://pi.dev/packages/pi-smart-router?name=router&type=extension) (12-step local pipeline, no LLM, local tier, formula-based cost estimate). **Different category** — [CC-Switch](https://github.com/farion1231/cc-switch) is a desktop app for manually switching provider configs between sessions — it can coexist with per-turn routing.
- **Related project** — [dsh-shift-router](https://github.com/green-dalii/dsh-shift-router), the DeepSeek Harness adaptation of pi-shift-router.
